analysis.one_liner: Lets mining claim holders occupy and build roads, pipelines, and facilities on public land even without a proven mineral find.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee markup or a floor vote in the Senate; it sat in the Energy Committee after one December 2023 subcommittee hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: Under a federal court ruling, holding a mining claim on public land only gives a company the right to use that land if it has actually discovered a valuable mineral deposit. This bill would flip that: claim holders could use, occupy, and build roads, transmission lines, pipelines, and other support facilities on public land whether or not any valuable mineral was ever found. It would also declare that the small annual claim fees miners already pay count as paying 'fair market value' for the use of public land. The bill never advanced past a subcommittee hearing.
analysis.who_benefits: Hardrock mining companies and anyone holding mining claims on federal land. They would gain guaranteed, indefinite rights to occupy and build on public land at low annual per-claim fees, with legal certainty that those rights survive even without a proven mineral deposit, and without a separate fair-market-value payment for the land they occupy.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hardrock mining companies and claim holders

how_it_helps.text: Gives claimants a statutory right to 'use, occupy, and conduct operations' on public land with or without discovery of a valuable mineral deposit, including building roads, transmission lines, pipelines, and other infrastructure on public land for support facilities.

Declares that a claimant who pays the required location and claim-maintenance fees is 'deemed to satisfy' the Federal Land Policy and Management Act's requirement to pay fair market value for the use of public land and resources — meaning the existing modest claim fees, not a market-based payment, settle the land-use obligation.
Includes a savings clause stating the bill does not diminish any existing right of entry, use, or occupancy of a claimant, and covers activities 'reasonably incident' to mining wherever they occur.

analysis.who_pays: The American public. Public lands would remain subject to mining-claim occupation and industrial support construction at minimal cost to the companies, with no market-value payment for the land itself, and other public-land users would share that space with facilities built for claims that may never produce anything.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public that owns federal land

drawbacks.text: The bill grants long-term occupation and construction rights on public land without requiring any proof that a valuable mineral deposit exists, so land could be tied up indefinitely by claims that never produce anything.

By deeming annual claim fees sufficient to meet the fair-market-value requirement, the bill lets companies lock in the use of public land for a few hundred dollars per claim per year rather than a market-based payment; claimants who qualify for the small-operator waiver would not even owe the maintenance fee.
The savings clause explicitly preserves every existing claimant right and the bill adds no new environmental or reclamation standard, so it expands industry rights without adding public protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine benefit is legal certainty: mining companies get clear rights to build the roads, power lines, and facilities any mine needs, after a court ruling had clouded those rights. But the bill goes further than clarity — it authorizes occupation and construction with no mineral discovery required, prices that occupation at nominal claim fees, and adds no new public-side protections. An honest supporter would have to concede that it transfers long-term control over public land to private claim holders at very little cost to them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which held one subcommittee hearing in December 2023 but never scheduled a markup or a floor vote, and the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada introduced the bill on April 25, 2023, joined by cosponsors from both parties: Republicans Mike Risch and Mike Crapo of Idaho, independent Kyrsten Sinema of Arizona, and Democrat Jacky Rosen of Nevada.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
On December 12, 2023, the committee's Subcommittee on Public Lands, Forests, and Mining held a hearing on the bill.
The full committee never reported the bill and the Senate never voted on it; no further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public is better off because the bill died: federal land stays under current law, where mining-claim holders must show a valuable mineral deposit before claiming broad rights to occupy and build on public land, and companies did not gain the expanded, fee-priced rights they sought.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship crossed party lines — a Nevada Democrat introduced the bill and three Republicans, one independent, and one Democrat cosponsored it — but no vote was ever recorded on the bill in committee or on the floor.

industries.note: The bill would give miners guaranteed rights to occupy and build on public land with or without a proven mineral find, and declare small annual claim fees sufficient to meet the fair-market-value requirement. The industry's gain comes directly at the expense of the public's ownership interest in federal land and of other land users.

industries.industry: Public lands users (recreation, ranching, conservation interests)
industries.note: Mining-claim holders could occupy and construct roads, pipelines, and support facilities on public land regardless of mineral discovery, shrinking the space and value of land held for the public.
